screens.title: Swift Fundamentals for iOS Development
screens.subtitle: Variables, types, optionals, control flow, functions, and value vs reference types

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson we will explore the essential building blocks of Swift that you’ll use every day while building iOS apps. You will learn how to declare constants and variables, why Swift’s type safety matters, and how optionals help you avoid common runtime errors. We’ll walk through control flow with conditional statements and loops, show how to write simple functions that accept parameters and return values, and explain the practical differences between structs and classes so you can make safer design choices. For example, you’ll see why a user model might be a struct to avoid unintended shared state, while a coordinator or view controller often fits a class because it represents shared, mutable resources. Along the way I’ll point out common mistakes, like forgetting to unwrap optionals or mixing value and reference expectations. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to read and write readable Swift snippets in a Playground, reason about when nil can appear, and choose between var and let deliberately. Keep an eye on the short code examples as concrete patterns you can copy into Playgrounds and experiment with. Ready to start? Notice how each small rule increases safety and predictability in your app code—what will you try first in a Playground?

keyIdea.title: Why these fundamentals matter
keyIdea.text: Mastering variables, types, optionals, control flow, and the class/struct distinction helps you write safer, clearer, and more predictable iOS code.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map directly to hands-on skills you will practice in a Playground. First, you will learn to declare and use variables and constants with var and let, and understand why preferring constants reduces bugs. Second, you will identify and use common Swift types — String, Int, Double, and Bool — and recognize when the compiler infers a type versus when you should annotate it explicitly. Third, you will safely work with optionals by unwrapping them with techniques such as optional binding and nil coalescing, so your code does not crash when values are missing. Fourth, you will write basic control flow using if/else and for-in loops to make decisions and iterate collections, and you will write simple functions that accept parameters and return values. Finally, you will compare classes and structs, and pick the right one for your data models. Each objective is paired with a milestone you can verify by running the provided Playground snippets and observing expected results. Practice each objective, and you’ll build a foundation that helps you reason about correctness and safety in iOS code.

screens.title: Variables and Constants (var vs let)
screens.subtitle: Declare immutable and mutable storage safely

narration.text: Let's define what variables and constants give you in Swift. A constant declared with the let keyword cannot change after it's set. This immutability is an intentional safety mechanism: if a value should not change, expressing that intent prevents accidental modifications and can make reasoning about code far easier. A variable declared with var is mutable and can be reassigned as your program runs. For a real example, imagine an app name that never changes after build: declare it with let. For a live score that updates, use var. A common misconception is to overuse var out of habit; prefer let when possible. When you prefer constants, the compiler can also optimize code paths more effectively. Another important practice is to give names that communicate intent—use userScore for a changing value and appName for a constant. Finally, remember that let prevents reassignment but does not guarantee deep immutability for reference types: a let reference to a class still allows its internal properties to change if those properties are mutable. That contrast leads us into a later lesson about value and reference types. To check your understanding, try declaring both let and var in a Playground and attempt invalid reassignments to see compiler feedback. What did the compiler tell you, and how might that guidance prevent a bug in your app?

keyIdea.title: Let vs Var
keyIdea.text: Use let for fixed values and var for changing state. Prefer let to reduce accidental mutation and improve code clarity.

content.html:
Core Concept Variables and Constants

Declare immutable and mutable storage safely

Definition and example
// A constant string
let appName = "My Awesome App"

// A variable integer
var userScore = 0
userScore = 10

// Reassigning a let would cause a compile-time error
// appName = "New App Name"
Explanation
  • let creates an immutable binding; reassignment is not allowed and is caught at compile time.
  • var creates mutable storage suitable for state that changes during execution.
  • Prefer let for intent and safety; it reduces bugs caused by accidental mutation.
  • Note: let with class references prevents reassignment of the reference but not mutation of the referenced object.
Analogy & Example Card
Think of let as a fixed label and var as a sticky note you can change. Example: appName is a fixed label, userScore is a sticky note that updates during gameplay.
Key Takeaway

Prefer constants for values that don't change; use variables consciously for state that must change.

Common Mistake

Using var by default leads to accidental mutations. Choose let first, then switch to var only when needed.

screens.title: Common Data Types and Type Inference
screens.subtitle: String, Int, Double, Bool and when to annotate types

narration.text: Swift is type-safe and offers powerful type inference. That means the compiler tries to deduce the type from the value you assign. Common primitive types you'll use are String for text, Int for integers, Double for floating-point numbers, and Bool for logical true/false values. For example, assigning "Welcome!" to a let constant results in a String without you needing to write : String. Type annotations are useful when you want clarity or when a variable starts without an initial value. A practical example: one variable holds a temperature measured as a Double to preserve fractional values, while another stores a count as an Int. Misconceptions often come from expecting Int to auto-convert to Double or vice versa; Swift requires explicit conversion between these numeric types. When interoperability or precise decimal behavior matters, explicitly annotate types and convert intentionally. To practice, declare a mix of inferred and annotated variables in a Playground, then attempt an arithmetic operation mixing Int and Double and observe the compiler prompt to convert types. That deliberate conversion helps avoid subtle bugs related to numeric precision and unexpected truncation.

keyIdea.title: Type safety and inference
keyIdea.text: Let the compiler infer types when clear, but annotate when you need precision or when the variable starts without an initial value.

content.html:
Definition Common Data Types

String, Int, Double, Bool and type inference

Code examples
let message: String = "Welcome!"
var temperature: Double = 25.5
var count = 3          // inferred as Int
var isActive = true    // inferred as Bool

// Mixing Int and Double requires conversion
let total: Double = Double(count) + temperature
Explanation
  • Type inference reduces boilerplate while keeping code readable.
  • Explicit annotations improve clarity and avoid unintended conversions.
  • Numeric types do not implicitly coerce; convert explicitly when mixing types.
Small scenarios
A price field should likely be Double. A user age should usually be Int. Use Bool for flags like isAuthenticated. When precision matters, prefer explicit Double instead of relying on inference.
Pro Tip

Annotate types when a variable starts nil or when you expect different numeric types to be combined later.

Key Takeaway

Type safety prevents a large class of runtime errors; use inference thoughtfully and annotate when necessary.

screens.title: Optionals: Representing Absence Safely
screens.subtitle: Why optionals exist and how they prevent runtime errors

narration.text: Optionals are one of Swift’s most important safety features. An optional type, written with a question mark after the type name, indicates that a value may be present or may be nil. This explicitness forces you to consider the absence of a value and prevents the kind of null pointer exceptions common in other languages. For example, a username loaded from a network response might be optional until the response populates it. When you try to use an optional’s value, you must unwrap it safely; otherwise you only see an Optional wrapper when printing, or the compiler will prevent unsafe access. A simple technique is optional binding with if let, which unwraps the value for use within the conditional block. Another helpful operator is nil coalescing, which supplies a default value when an optional is nil. A common misconception is to force-unwrap optionals with a bang operator in production code; that can reintroduce crashes if the value is unexpectedly nil. Instead prefer optional binding or nil coalescing, and when needed use guard let to early-exit from functions. Try declaring an optional in a Playground, then practice both binding and coalescing to see how control flow differs when a value is present or missing. Which pattern will you choose for optional data in your app?

keyIdea.title: Optionals prevent nil crashes
keyIdea.text: Use optional binding and nil coalescing to handle missing values explicitly and avoid runtime errors.

content.html:
Core Concept Optionals

Represent absence safely with optionals

Code examples
var username: String? = "Alice"
var email: String?

if let unwrappedUsername = username {
  print("Welcome, \(unwrappedUsername)!")
} else {
  print("Please log in.")
}

let displayEmail = email ?? "No email provided"
print(displayEmail)
Explanation
  • Optionals model values that may be absent, using a clear syntax: Type?.
  • Optional binding (if let / guard let) unwraps safely and provides a non-optional value inside a controlled scope.
  • Nil coalescing supplies a default when the optional is nil, reducing branching in simple cases.
Scenario Card
Imagine loading a profile: email may be missing. Use optional binding to show the email only when present, or nil coalescing to display a default message when absent.
Common Mistake

Avoid force-unwrapping optionals in production code; it defeats the safety model and can crash your app.

Key Takeaway

Handle nil explicitly with binding or coalescing. Prefer safe unwrapping to keep apps stable.

screens.title: Optional Binding with if let and guard let
screens.subtitle: Two safe patterns to unwrap optionals

narration.text: Optional binding gives you controlled ways to access an optional’s value only when it exists. The if let pattern unwraps the optional and executes a block if the value is present. For example, if let name = username { use name } runs the block with a non-optional name. This is useful when you want to handle the present-case inline. Guard let is complementary: it unwraps at the start of a function or scope and exits early if the value is nil, keeping the happy path unindented and easier to read. For instance, guard let token = authToken else { return } ensures that subsequent code can use a non-optional token. A common misconception is that guard let is safer than if let; both are safe, but guard let encourages early exit and clearer flow in functions. Practice both patterns in Playgrounds: use if let when you are branching locally, and guard let to validate preconditions at the top of functions. Also note scoping rules: values bound by if let are available only inside the if block, while guard let bindings are available after the guard statement for the remaining scope. Which pattern makes your function body simpler and more readable?

keyIdea.title: Choose binding by flow
keyIdea.text: Use if let for local conditional handling and guard let to assert preconditions and keep the main path unindented.

content.html:
Process Flow Optional Binding Patterns

if let and guard let for safe unwrapping

If let example
if let unwrappedName = username {
  print("Welcome, \(unwrappedName)!")
} else {
  print("Please log in.")
}
Guard let example
func submitForm(name: String?) {
  guard let name = name else {
    print("Name is required")
    return
  }
  // name is non-optional here
  print("Submitting for \(name)")
}
Why use guard let?
Guard let reduces nesting and clearly expresses preconditions. Use it at the top of functions when a missing value means early return.
Misconception Check

Both patterns are safe. Choose based on clarity: if let for local branching, guard let for validating preconditions.

Try This

Refactor a small function to use guard let and notice how its happy path becomes more readable.

screens.title: Nil Coalescing and Providing Defaults
screens.subtitle: Use ?? to fall back when an optional is nil

narration.text: Nil coalescing is a compact way to provide a default when an optional is nil. The operator reads as: if the optional has a value, use it; otherwise, use the default on the right-hand side. This is useful when a missing value should be replaced with a sensible fallback, such as displaying "No email provided" when an email is nil. Nil coalescing reduces the need for verbose branching when a default is acceptable. However, avoid overusing it where you must distinguish between absence and a default value; in those cases, explicit conditional handling is better. For example, defaulting an optional timestamp to the current time might hide the fact that data was never supplied. Practice in a Playground by declaring an optional and using nil coalescing to display a message. Then contrast that with optional binding to see where the default hides missing data. A quick mental check: if the app must react differently when a value is absent versus present, favor binding. If absent implies a clear default that requires no special handling, nil coalescing offers concise, readable code.

keyIdea.title: Use ?? selectively
keyIdea.text: Nil coalescing gives a compact default. Use it when a fallback is acceptable, and use binding when absence requires distinct handling.

content.html:
Definition Nil Coalescing

Provide a concise default when an optional is nil

Code example
var email: String?
let displayEmail = email ?? "No email provided"
print(displayEmail)
When to use
  • Use when a reasonable default exists and absence does not require special handling.
  • Avoid when you must detect missing data or when the default would mask a bug.
Scenario
Showing "No email provided" in a profile is a good use of nil coalescing. Defaulting a missing server timestamp to now might hide synchronization issues, so avoid coalescing in that case.
Key Takeaway

Nil coalescing is concise for defaults; use binding when absence needs explicit branching.

screens.title: Control Flow: if/else and for-in loops
screens.subtitle: Make decisions and iterate collections

narration.text: Control flow constructs let you direct how your code executes. The if/else statement evaluates a Boolean condition and runs different blocks depending on the outcome. Use it to handle branches like authenticated versus unauthenticated users. For example, if isAuthenticated { show dashboard } else { show login }. For iteration, the for-in loop walks over a sequence such as a range or an array and executes code for each element. Use for-in to process each item in a list, for example printing each fruit in an array. A common beginner mistake is modifying a collection while iterating it; avoid mutating the container directly during iteration or iterate over a copy. Also be careful with off-by-one errors when constructing ranges; Swift offers closed ranges 1...5 and half-open ranges 0..<5. Practice writing short loops in a Playground: iterate an array of strings, build a result array using append, and print each step. These constructs are the basis for most application logic, from validation to UI updates, so mastering them enables you to express app behavior clearly and predictably. Control Flow: if/else and for-in loops means if/else handles branching; for-in iterates sequences. avoid mutating a collection while iterating it.. In practical terms, make decisions and iterate collections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decisions and repetition
keyIdea.text: if/else handles branching; for-in iterates sequences. Avoid mutating a collection while iterating it.

content.html:
Core Concept Control Flow

if/else and for-in loops

Examples
let isAuthenticated = true
if isAuthenticated {
  print("User is logged in.")
} else {
  print("User needs to authenticate.")
}

for i in 1...5 {
  print("Count: \(i)")
}

let fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"]
for fruit in fruits {
  print("I like \(fruit)")
}
Best practices
  • Avoid mutating the collection you are iterating; iterate over a copy if you must remove items.
  • Prefer clear boolean names like isAuthenticated for readable conditions.
  • Use ranges intentionally and be aware of closed vs half-open ranges.
Analogy
Think of if/else as a forked road and for-in as repeating the same step for each passenger in a queue.
Try This

Create a loop that filters an array by condition and builds a new array with matching items. Observe whether you mutate the original array.

screens.title: Functions: Define and Call with Parameters and Returns
screens.subtitle: Encapsulate logic with named, reusable code blocks

narration.text: Functions let you encapsulate a task, name it, and reuse it throughout your app. A function has a name, zero or more parameters, and an optional return type. For example, a function that computes a rectangle area accepts width and height parameters and returns their product. This promotes clarity and avoids duplicating logic. A common mistake is writing very large functions that do many things; prefer small functions with a single responsibility. When naming functions, choose verbs that describe the action, like calculateRectangleArea. Also think about argument labels to make calls read naturally. Practice by putting a few functions into a Playground: define one that returns a Double and call it with different numeric arguments. Try edge cases, such as zero dimensions, to see how your function behaves. Finally, consider whether a function should be mutating when attached to a struct, or whether it should return a new value. Returning values instead of mutating state often leads to easier-to-test code. What small function could you extract from a repetitive code block in your project? Functions: Define and Call with Parameters and Returns means write small, well-named functions that accept parameters and return results. prefer single responsibility and testable outputs.. In practical terms, encapsulate logic with named, reusable code blocks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Functions for reuse
keyIdea.text: Write small, well-named functions that accept parameters and return results. Prefer single responsibility and testable outputs.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough Functions

Define and call functions with parameters and return values

Function example
func calculateRectangleArea(width: Double, height: Double) -> Double {
  return width * height
}

let area1 = calculateRectangleArea(width: 10.0, height: 5.0)
print("Area 1: \(area1)")

let area2 = calculateRectangleArea(width: 7.5, height: 3.2)
print("Area 2: \(area2)")
Explanation
  • Functions encapsulate logic; give them a single responsibility and a clear name.
  • Use typed parameters and a typed return to keep contracts explicit and predictable.
  • Prefer returning values for easier testing; mutate state only when appropriate.
Analogy
Think of a function as a recipe: inputs are ingredients, the function is the cooking, and the return value is the finished dish.
Pro Tip

Name functions so calls read naturally, for example: calculateRectangleArea(width:height:).

Key Takeaway

Small, well-typed functions make code easier to reason about and test in Playgrounds.

screens.title: Structs and Classes: Value vs Reference
screens.subtitle: When to use structs and when to use classes

narration.text: Both structs and classes let you define custom types, but their fundamental behavior differs: structs are value types and classes are reference types. With a struct, assigning it to a new variable creates a copy; changes to the new copy do not affect the original. With a class, assigning a reference creates another pointer to the same instance; changes through any reference are visible everywhere. For example, a Point struct copied and modified does not change the original, whereas changing a Person class property via a second reference alters the same underlying object. In iOS, structs are commonly used for data models and SwiftUI views because value semantics avoid accidental shared state and are often more predictable. Classes are appropriate for shared resources, controllers, and objects that need inheritance or identity. A common error is expecting a struct to behave like a class or vice versa; test your assumptions by assigning and mutating instances in a Playground. Ask yourself whether your type needs identity and shared mutable state; if not, prefer struct. This choice affects performance, testability, and the clarity of your program's behavior.

keyIdea.title: Value vs Reference
keyIdea.text: Structs copy on assignment; classes share references. Choose structs for independent copies and classes for shared, identity-bearing objects.

content.html:
Comparison Struct vs Class

Value and reference semantics explained

Struct example (value type)
struct Point {
  var x: Int
  var y: Int
}

var p1 = Point(x: 10, y: 20)
var p2 = p1 // copy
p2.x = 30
print("p1.x: \(p1.x), p2.x: \(p2.x)") // 10, 30
Class example (reference type)
class Person {
  var name: String
  init(name: String) { self.name = name }
}

let person1 = Person(name: "Charlie")
let person2 = person1 // reference
person2.name = "David"
print("person1.name: \(person1.name), person2.name: \(person2.name)") // David, David
When to use Struct

Prefer for small data models where copies are acceptable and predictable behavior is desired.

When to use Class

Use when you need shared mutable state, identity, or inheritance, such as view controllers or coordinators.

Misconception

Choosing class for convenience can introduce hard-to-find bugs due to shared state; always question whether identity is required.

screens.title: Playground Lab: Experiment with Optionals and Functions
screens.subtitle: Step through the guided Playground tasks

narration.text: This lab guides you through three short experiments in a Playground that reinforce optionals and functions. First, declare an optional string and print its direct value to observe the Optional wrapper. Then safely unwrap it using if let and print a personalized greeting when present, otherwise a fallback. Second, assign nil to the optional and re-run the binding to see the else branch execute. Third, write a simple function that accepts width and height and returns the area. Call that function with different numeric types and explicitly convert Int to Double when necessary. These steps show how optionals change control flow and how functions encapsulate logic. A common beginner trap is reading the Optional wrapper as the value; the binding pattern shows how to access the real value. When testing, add prints after each operation to observe results in the Playground's results pane. This iterative experimentation is the fastest way to internalize safety patterns and function contracts. Which output surprised you when you first ran similar code, and why? Playground Lab: Experiment with Optionals and Functions means run small, focused playground experiments: observe optional wrappers, practice binding, and test function calls with type conversions.. In practical terms, step through the guided playground tasks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Experiment to learn
keyIdea.text: Run small, focused Playground experiments: observe Optional wrappers, practice binding, and test function calls with type conversions.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity Playground Lab

Experiment with Optionals and Functions

Starter Playground code
// Declare an optional
var userName: String? = "Alex"
print("Direct print: \(userName)")

// Optional binding
if let name = userName {
  print("Hello, \(name)!")
} else {
  print("User name is not set.")
}

// Assign nil and try again
userName = nil
if let name = userName {
  print("Hello, \(name)!")
} else {
  print("User name is not set after being set to nil.")
}

// Function example
func calculateRectangleArea(width: Double, height: Double) -> Double {
  return width * height
}
let area1 = calculateRectangleArea(width: 10.0, height: 5.0)
print("Area 1: \(area1)")
Guided steps
  1. Run the code and observe Optional("Alex") printed directly, then a clean greeting from binding.
  2. Set the optional to nil and observe the else path output.
  3. Call the function with different values and confirm numeric conversion when mixing types.
Reflection
Note how binding clarifies where values exist and how functions return predictable outputs. These experiments reveal language guarantees and compiler guidance.
Key Takeaway

Small, repeatable tests in Playgrounds solidify understanding of optionals and functions quickly.

screens.title: Common Assessment: Constants, Optionals, and Structs
screens.subtitle: Sample questions and reasoning checks

narration.text: A short assessment helps confirm conceptual understanding. One common question asks what happens if you uncomment a reassignment to a let constant: the compiler raises a compile-time error because a constant cannot be reassigned. This checks whether you grasp immutability. Another question asks whether to use a struct or class when you need a copy-on-assignment behavior for a Book model; the correct answer is struct, because it creates independent copies on assignment. These questions test both syntax and semantics. When you practice, always explain not only which answer is correct but why alternatives are incorrect. For example, an optional being a let still means its binding is immutable; you cannot change the binding, but the wrapped value behavior depends on whether the type is a value or reference type. Also, consider corner cases in functions: what should a function return when inputs are invalid? Include guard let or return an optional to express that clearly. Assessments that mix small code examples with short explanations are most revealing because they force you to think about both behavior and intent. Common Assessment: Constants, Optionals, and Structs means test both syntax (what compiles) and semantics (what values and side effects actually occur) to ensure deep understanding.. In practical terms, sample questions and reasoning checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Assessment focus
keyIdea.text: Test both syntax (what compiles) and semantics (what values and side effects actually occur) to ensure deep understanding.

content.html:
Assessment Idea Check understanding with short questions

Common Assessment: Constants, Optionals, and Structs

Sample Question 1
Given var city: String = "New York" and let country: String? = "USA", what happens if you try to reassign country? Explain why. Correct answer: compile-time error because country is a constant declared with let.
Sample Question 2
Which construct ensures copies are independent when passed around: class or struct? Explain the difference in behavior on assignment. Correct answer: struct, because it is a value type and assignment creates a copy.
Why these questions work

They require both factual recall and reasoning about consequences — the heart of programming competence.

Key Takeaway

Explain not just the result but the why. That reveals true understanding of semantics, not just syntax.

screens.title: Live-Coding Demo Plan: From var/let to Playground Video
screens.subtitle: Plan a 15-minute demo that teaches these fundamentals

narration.text: This slide outlines a practical plan for a 15-minute live-coding demo using a Playground. Start by explaining var versus let with two examples: an immutable app name and a mutable user score. Next, show String, Int, Double, and Bool examples and demonstrate type inference and explicit annotations. narration.text: Let's summarize the essential points to remember. First, prefer let for values that don't change and use var only when you need mutability. Second, Swift’s type safety is a feature: allow the compiler to infer types when clear, but annotate when you need precision or when a variable starts nil. Third, optionals model absence explicitly; use if let, guard let, or nil coalescing to handle optional values safely and avoid crashes. Fourth, control flow constructs like if/else and for-in let you direct logic and process collections; be careful not to mutate collections while iterating. Fifth, write small, well-named functions that accept parameters and return values to improve reuse and testability. Finally, understand that structs are value types and classes are reference types; choose based on whether you need independent copies or shared identity. let vs var

Optionals

Structs vs Classes
